messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL matches the DOI given in the source (10.1016/j.watres.2021.117677; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2021.117677).

Text states the study is a field demonstration of a hybrid NF/UV-sulfite treatment train for AFFF-impacted groundwater and that PFASs are concentrated in the NF reject, which is then UV treated (S04-E01, S04-E04). This supports groundwater as the matrix and NF reject as the treated concentrate.

Methods describe groundwater pumped to a storage tank, then through sediment and cation exchange pretreatment, then to an NF system (three 2540 NF270 membranes) operated to 90% recovery, producing a 10% reject that is transferred to a 57 L UV reactor tank, amended with ~10 mM sulfite and NaOH for pH adjustment, UV-treated for 23 h, and all treated water polished by GAC before discharge (S04-E04, S04-E05, S04-E06). This matches the treatment train description.

The study is explicitly described as a "field demonstration pilot-scale hybrid NF/UV-sulfite treatment train" (S04-E01). It also notes performance sustained throughout a 30-day consecutive field trial (S04-E01) and that one treatment cycle was conducted per day during the field deployment (S04-E06), supporting the scale and duration description.
The article describes a "field demonstration pilot-scale" treatment train (S04-E01), which aligns with categorization as pilot_or_field_deployment.

The first endpoint concerns NF performance. The conclusion notes that high-pressure membranes achieved good PFAS rejection (≥95%) at high permeate recoveries and that PFASs were concentrated in the NF reject stream (S04-E01, S04-E08). This is a separation process endpoint, so endpoint_type="separation" is appropriate.

The second endpoint refers to UV-sulfite treatment of the NF reject, with the conclusion stating "PFAS destruction was accomplished by UV treatment after amending the NF reject with sulfite photosensitizer ... and adjusting to alkaline pH conditions (pH 11.2)" (S04-E01). This is a destruction endpoint based on parent-compound loss, so endpoint_type="destruction" is consistent with the source.

The third endpoint summarizes overall PFAS removal by the hybrid train. The conclusion states the study reports a hybrid NF/UV-sulfite treatment train for the separation and destruction of PFASs from groundwater, concentrating PFASs in a reject stream and then achieving destruction via UV-sulfite, with all treated water passed through GAC (S04-E01, S04-E04, S04-E08). This is properly categorized as an overall removal endpoint.

Text reports good PFAS rejection (≥95%) by high-pressure membranes during the pilot and that PFASs were concentrated in the NF reject stream, reducing the volume requiring further treatment (S04-E01). Rejection of individual PFASs over 30 cycles averaged 92–98% (S04-E08). This supports the interpretation and reported term of PFAS rejection by NF as a separation endpoint.

Conclusion states "PFAS destruction was accomplished by UV treatment after amending the NF reject with sulfite photosensitizer ... and adjusting to alkaline pH conditions (pH 11.2)" with rates consistent with small-scale studies (S04-E01). The interpretation that destruction is based on parent-compound loss rather than mineralization is consistent with the provided text; mineralization is not claimed. Reported term and interpretation are supported.

The study describes a hybrid NF/UV-sulfite train in which NF separates PFASs into a small-volume reject, which is then destructively treated by UV-sulfite, and notes that all treated water (NF permeate and UV-treated reject) is passed through a GAC polishing filter prior to discharge (S04-E01, S04-E04, S04-E08). This supports the overall PFAS removal interpretation and reported term.

Text notes that PFASs evaluated in the study have molecular weights 250–500 g/mol (S04-E02) and describes differing rejection for longer vs shorter chain PFASs (S04-E08). This supports the description of multiple PFASs with MW 250–500 g/mol and varying chain lengths being evaluated.
The conclusion explicitly states, "High-pressure membranes are not frequently used for PFAS treatment due to concentrate management challenges" (S04-E01), matching the author-reported limitation.

The conclusion states that "pH adjustment to 11.2 and subsequent neutralization may incur additional operating challenges and costs" (S04-E01), matching the author-reported limitation about pH adjustment and neutralization.

Design details show the study is a pilot-scale field demonstration at a specific AFFF-impacted groundwater site, using a custom high-pressure system with three 2540 NF270 membranes under defined conditions (S04-E01, S04-E03, S04-E04, S04-E05). From these explicit design facts, the inference that results may not directly generalize to other waters or membrane configurations is reasonable as a design_inferred limitation.

Methods and results note a temporary decrease in PFAS rejection around day 6 corresponding to delayed cation exchange cartridge filter change-out, leading to Ca2+ and Mg2+ breakthrough and reduced PFAS rejection (S04-E08). This supports the stated limitation about sensitivity of NF performance to pretreatment efficacy.
Methods state that 568 L (150 gal) of groundwater from the storage tank was pumped to the NF concentration tank per treatment cycle (S04-E04). This supports the value 568 L for batch volume to NF.
The batch volume is reported in liters (568 L) in the methods (S04-E04), so unit "L" is correct.
NF operation is described as treating 568 L batches to 90% total permeate recovery, yielding 57 L of reject (S04-E05, S04-E06). This supports the value 90 for permeate recovery per batch.
Permeate recovery is expressed as a percentage (e.g., 90% total permeate recovery) in the methods (S04-E05, S04-E06), so unit "%" is correct.
The NF pilot is used to treat 568 L batches to 90% recoveries, yielding 57 L of reject per cycle (S04-E05, S04-E06). This supports the reject volume value of 57 L.
Reject volume is given in liters (57 L) in the methods (S04-E05, S04-E06), so unit "L" is correct.

The NF pilot system is described as containing three 2540 (2.5" diameter × 40" length) spiral wound NF270 membranes (DuPont Filmtec) (S04-E05). This supports the stated membrane type and configuration.
Membrane type is descriptive and not numerical; leaving unit as null is appropriate.
